Empirical Research Plan: Minimum-Wage Effects on Restaurant Earnings & Employment, 1990q1–2006q2  

------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
   • Method: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study (dynamic DID) implemented on a county-quarter panel.  
   • Why appropriate?  
     – Policy variation is discrete (statutory minimum wage changes).  
     – Multiple treatments across states and time allow use of two-way and border-pair fixed effects.  
     – County-level QCEW data provide a long pre- and post-window for credible parallel-trend tests.  
     – Border-pair design further nets out spatial heterogeneity by comparing counties that share a labor market but face different statutory minima.  
   • Estimator: Sun & Abraham (2021) “interaction weighted” estimator to avoid biased weights in staggered treatment settings.  

------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  
   Treatment variable  
     T_it = log(real state minimum wage_it) – log(real federal minimum wage_t)  
     (or indicator 1{state min > federal}). The preferred specification uses the continuous log gap.  

   Control group / Counterfactual  
     – Main specification: Untreated counties in the same quarter whose state minimum did not change.  
     – Preferred: The bordering county on the other side of the state line (within each matched pair) that did not experience the same change (“border-pair DID”).  

   Treatment timing  
     q* = first quarter in which the new state minimum became effective. Event-time k = q – q*.  

   Running variable and cutoff  
     – Not an RDD; no running variable.  

------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

   A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of the policy, treated and control counties would have followed the same employment/earnings paths.  
        Plausibility: More credible inside narrow border pairs: economic shocks (tourism, agriculture, weather) are highly correlated across the state line.  

   A2. No spillovers/SUTVA: A change in State A’s minimum does not directly affect employment in the adjacent State B county.  
        Plausibility: Some commuting spillovers exist but are muted because restaurants are local-consumption industries; we will test sensitivity to distance ≤ 10 miles from the border.  

   A3. No differential policy anticipation: Firms do not adjust prior to the legal effective date.  
        Plausibility: Implementation lags are short (1–3 months). We will include leads of treatment in the event study to test for anticipatory effects.  

   A4. Exogeneity of policy with respect to county-level restaurant shocks conditional on state × year and county fixed effects.  
        Plausibility: State politics drive adoption more than county restaurant conditions. Border-pair design further purges shocks common to the local labor market.  

------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats & Mitigation  

   T1. Differential regional trends unrelated to the minimum wage.  
       – Mitigation: (i) border-pair FE; (ii) county-specific linear trends; (iii) interacting Census-division × quarter fixed effects.  

   T2. Policy endogeneity to state business cycles (states raise the minimum when labor markets are tight).  
       – Mitigation: (i) Include state-specific time trends; (ii) instrument the state minimum with the average of neighboring states’ minimums lagged one year (political diffusion IV) as a robustness check.  

   T3. Cross-border commuting / spillovers.  
       – Mitigation: (i) Drop metro areas where >20% of workers commute across the state line; (ii) test distance-band heterogeneity (<5, 5–10, 10–25 miles).  

------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline  

```r
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)   # fast data manipulation
library(fixest)       # TWFE and Sun-Abraham estimator
library(haven)        # if Stata dta files are used
library(did)          # Callaway & Sant’Anna implementation
library(modelsummary) # quick tables

# 1. Load Data ----------------------------------------------------------
qcew <- fread("qcew_restaurants_1990_2006.csv")   # county-qtr panel
mw    <- fread("state_minwage_qtr_1990_2006.csv") # min-wage by state & qtr
border<- fread("border_pairs.csv")                # county_id, pair_id

# 2. Merge & Construct Variables ---------------------------------------
dt <- merge(qcew, mw, by = c("state","quarter"))

# real minimum wage in 2006 dollars
dt[, real_mw := state_minwage / cpi_qtr ]
dt[, real_fed := fed_minwage   / cpi_qtr ]
dt[, mw_gap   := log(real_mw) - log(real_fed)]

# treatment timing: first quarter when gap > 0 after being =0
setorder(dt, county, quarter)
dt[, treat := as.integer(mw_gap > 0)]
dt[, first_treat_qtr := ifelse(any(treat==1),
                               quarter[which(treat==1)[1]], NA),
   by = county]

# Event time k = -4 ... +8 (set to NA for never-treated)
dt[, event_time := quarter - first_treat_qtr]

# Keep balanced panel
dt <- dt[complete.cases(emp)]

# Merge border-pair id
dt <- merge(dt, border, by = "county_id", all.x = TRUE)

# 3. Main Specification -------------------------------------------------
# TWFE with county and quarter FE, clustered by state
spec1 <- feols(
  l_emp ~ mw_gap | county + quarter, 
  data = dt[state_minwage_change!=0 | mw_gap==0],
  cluster = ~state
)

# 4. Border-Pair DID ----------------------------------------------------
spec2 <- feols(
  l_emp ~ mw_gap | pair_id + quarter, 
  data = dt[!is.na(pair_id)],
  cluster = ~pair_id
)

# 5. Event-Study (Sun & Abraham) ---------------------------------------
dt_sa <- att_gt(yname = "l_emp",
                tname = "quarter",
                idname = "county",
                gname = "first_treat_qtr",
                xformla = ~1,
                data = dt)

es <- aggte(dt_sa, type = "dynamic", min_e = -8, max_e = 8)

# 6. Robustness: County-specific trends --------------------------------
spec3 <- feols(
  l_emp ~ mw_gap + i(quarter, county, ref = 1) | county + quarter, 
  data = dt, cluster = ~state
)

# 7. Output -------------------------------------------------------------
modelsummary(list("TWFE" = spec1, "Border FE" = spec2, 
                  "County trend" = spec3),
             gof_omit = 'Adj|Within',
             stars = TRUE)
```
Notes:  
l_emp = log(employment). Repeat for log average weekly earnings. Robustness checks: (i) drop quarters within ±2 qtrs of federal hikes; (ii) placebo on manufacturing (expected zero effect).  

------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  

Earnings: A statutory $1 (≈14% in 2000) increase should raise average restaurant weekly earnings roughly 4–6% (pass-through is attenuated because many workers already earn above the old minimum).  

Employment: Theory with monopsony predicts small negative or zero effects; competitive model predicts elasticity about −0.1. Prior: a 10% increase in the minimum will change restaurant employment by between −2% and 0% (elasticity −0.2 to 0). My central prior: −0.05 elasticity (statistically indistinguishable from zero).  

------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  

C1. Pre-treatment parallel trends verified by lead coefficients ….. 1  
C2. No anticipation effects (leads insignificant) …………………….. 1  
C3. No spillovers across units (SUTVA) ……………………………….. 0  
C4. Exogenous treatment timing conditional on FE ………………… 0  
C5. Stable composition of units (no mass county reclassification) … 1  

Total = 3 / 5. We view the design as moderately credible; remaining concerns will be probed with robustness and IV-style falsification.
